Introduction Deep neural networks (DNNs) [22] have driven major advances in computer vision, achieving state-of-the-art performance across image classification [33], object detection [51, 52], semantic segmentation, and dense prediction tasks [42, 53].

Despite this progress, vision models frequently produce overconfident and poorly calibrated predictions [24], even when confronted with ambiguous inputs, corrupted samples, or out-of-distribution data [27].

evidence.quote: We evaluate the proposed approach across classification, semantic segmentation, and out-of-distribution detection using convolutional and transformer-based architectures on diverse datasets.

Across these settings, stochastic activation switching improves uncertainty quality while preserving competitive primary-task performance, showing that stochastic nonlinearities provide an effective and information-preserving source of predictive variation for visual recognition.

limitations.summary: Across classification, segmentation, and out-of-distribution detection experiments, the proposed approach improves uncertainty quality without degrading the main task performance, and remains effective across different visual domains and architectures.

A limitation is that the activation pair influences the trade-off between predictive performance and calibration, while repeated stochastic passes introduce additional inference cost.
Future work can explore adaptive activation selection and more efficient sampling strategies to reduce inference overhead while preserving uncertainty estimation quality.
